nameStory: Coral honeysuckle gets its name from its stunning coral-red tubular flowers that look like tiny trumpets. The 'honeysuckle' part comes from the sweet nectar hidden inside these trumpet-shaped blooms, which has delighted generations of children (and hummingbirds!) who carefully pulled the flowers apart to taste the droplets of natural sweetness.
description: Coral honeysuckle is a beautiful native climbing vine that can reach 10-20 feet in length as it scrambles up trees, fences, or trellises. Its most striking feature is clusters of brilliant coral-red to orange-red tubular flowers that bloom from late spring through summer. The vine has smooth, oval leaves that are blue-green in color, and unlike many honeysuckles, it's not aggressively invasive. This well-behaved native is a hummingbird magnet and makes an excellent choice for wildlife gardens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright coral-red to orange-red tubular flowers about 1-2 inches long, clustered at branch tips. The flowers have no fragrance (unlike many honeysuckles) and feel waxy to the touch with five small lobes at the opening.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. The uppermost pairs are fused together around the stem, creating what looks like a single leaf with the stem passing through the middle. Leaves feel smooth and have a blue-green color with a waxy coating.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing or trailing vine that twines around supports without tendrils. Stems are smooth and somewhat woody, feeling firm but flexible when bent.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small bright red berries in clusters, appearing in late summer. The berries are about 1/4 inch across and feel soft when ripe, though they're not particularly tasty to humans.

habitat: Coral honeysuckle thrives in woodland edges, clearings, and partly shaded areas throughout New England, though it's more common in the southern parts of the region. It prefers well-drained soil and can tolerate both acidic and slightly alkaline conditions. You'll often find it growing along forest borders, climbing up into small trees or sprawling over rocks and fallen logs.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in early spring, followed by the first flush of coral-red flowers in late spring. This is when the vine is most noticeable as the bright blooms stand out against the fresh green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with clusters of trumpet flowers attracting hummingbirds throughout the season. The vine continues to produce new flowers into late summer.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and leaves may turn yellowish before dropping. The berries often persist after leaves fall, providing food for birds.
seasonality.winter: Woody stems remain visible, and you can still identify the vine by its smooth bark and the distinctive way upper leaves remain fused around the stem on persistent twigs.

funFact: Coral honeysuckle flowers are perfectly designed for hummingbirds - their long, narrow tubes match the length of a hummingbird's beak and tongue, and the coral-red color is in the exact wavelength range that hummingbirds see best, while the complete lack of fragrance means they haven't 'wasted' energy attracting other pollinators!
confusionNotes: The biggest confusion is with invasive Japanese honeysuckle, but coral honeysuckle has scentless coral-red flowers (not fragrant white-to-yellow ones) and blue-green leaves that are fused around the stem at the top. Memory trick: 'Coral for native, fragrant for foreign' - if it smells sweet, it's probably the invasive Japanese species.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of the 'good guy' honeysuckles - many people don't realize that several honeysuckle species in New England are aggressive invasives from Asia, while coral honeysuckle is a well-behaved native that actually supports local wildlife. When someone says they're removing honeysuckle, make sure they're not accidentally targeting this beneficial native species!
compareHints: Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem. Japanese honeysuckle has fragrant white-to-yellow flowers, while the shrubby honeysuckles like Morrow's and Tatarian don't climb and have much smaller paired flowers. The native fly honeysuckles have yellow flowers and grow as upright shrubs, not climbing vines.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
